concept.name: Exhaustion
concept.definition: The fading of aggressive order flow near the end of a move: successive pushes in the trend direction are made on shrinking market-order volume, showing that the initiating side is running out of participants willing to chase the price. On a footprint it appears as very small traded volume at the bar extreme compared with earlier bars in the move.
concept.intuition: The auction runs out of bidders: price may still tick to a new extreme, but almost nobody is left willing to trade there.
concept.mechanics: Read by comparing traded volume (or delta) at successive price extremes within a move — e.g., a new high made on a fraction of the market-buy volume of prior highs — often combined with delta divergence and a stalling of price progress.
concept.failure_modes: Exhaustion readings are invisible without quality tick data and are confounded by time-of-day liquidity cycles; a paused initiative side can reload at any time, so exhaustion marks vulnerability, not a guaranteed turn.
concept.misconceptions: Exhaustion is not the same as a reversal signal — a move can end by drifting sideways for hours after exhaustion, and fading the first sign of weak volume at an extreme is a common way to get run over by trend days.
concept.example: ES makes a new session high, but only 48 market buy orders print at the top of the bar versus 600–900 at prior highs; the buyers are read as exhausted and price rotates back down.

citations.source: ATAS — How to read the order flow (buyers 'exhausted' — insignificant buy volume at the high)
